title: Game 3: Magnus vs Hans
notes: Game 3 of 12 in the experiment, from the Italian Game. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

I avoided the sharp 5.d4 exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ complications and the losing 5.Nxe5 Nxe5 6.d4 trick, choosing instead the solid 5.d3 which supports e4, opens the c1-bishop, and leaves no piece of mine undefended or hit by a pawn push.

White's quiet 5.d3 just solidifies the center, so I should complete development rather than grab material — Bxf2+ or Nxe4 simply lose a piece to Kxf2/dxe4. Castling is safe since f7 stays defended by the rook and any Ng5 can be met with h6, and it keeps the option of d6 or d5 next.

Bxf7+ just loses a bishop to Rxf7, and Nxe5 drops a piece to Nxe5, so I ignore those; Black's main freeing idea is ...d5 hitting my c4 bishop, which I can meet with exd5 once my king is safe. I'll complete development with the natural, solid castling move.

This is the Giuoco Pianissimo, and I want a solid setup rather than a tactical adventure — Bxf2+ followed by Nxe4 just loses a piece for a pawn after Rxf2 and dxe4. Playing d6 bolsters my e5 pawn, opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, and keeps Bg4/Be6 and Ne7-g6 regrouping options available.

Bxf7+ is a blunder since Rxf7 just wins the bishop for a pawn, so I stick to normal Giuoco Pianissimo development. My c4 bishop is my loosest piece and sits on a diagonal where ...Na5 or a future ...d5/...b5 could harass it, so I tuck it back to b3 where it stays safe, keeps the a2-g8 diagonal, and prepares Nbd2/Re1 and a later d4.

This is a Giuoco Pianissimo structure where my c5-bishop is the piece White wants to hit with d4 or Na4, so I want to keep it safe and flexible. Nxe4 just loses a piece to dxe4, and Bxf2+ is met by Rxf2 with no follow-up, so I play a6, giving the bishop the a7 retreat and preparing Be6/Ba7 with a solid setup.

The natural plan in this Italian structure is to strike in the centre with d4, hitting both e5 and the Bc5; after 8.d4 exd4 9.cxd4 the bishop must retreat and I gain central space with tempo. I checked Black's counter-tactics: 8...Nxe4 9.dxc5 dxc5 10.Qd5 regains the piece and a pawn, and 8...exd4 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 Bxd4 11.Qxd4 just wins a piece, so nothing is loose.

White has finally committed to d4, and I want to keep the tension while saving my bishop from being hit — 8...Bb6 retreats to a safe square where the bishop still eyes the d4/f2 diagonal. Captures don't work for White: 9.dxe5 dxe5 10.Nxe5? loses a piece to 10...Nxe5, and my own 8...Bxd4 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 just drops a piece for two pawns.

I checked that my b3 bishop is safely guarded by the a2 pawn and cannot be hit by ...d5, and that d4 has enough defenders (Qd1, Nf3) against ...exd4 and ...Nxd4 ideas. Re1 adds a second defender to e4 so that ...Nxe4 just drops a piece after Rxe4, and it develops my last inactive piece toward the center.

The center is tense but my e5 point is adequately defended, so I want a useful prophylactic move rather than releasing the tension with 9...exd4 or a risky 9...Bxd4 (which just loses a piece after 10.cxd4 Nxd4 11.Nxe5). 9...h6 stops Bg5 pinning my knight and Ng5 ideas, keeping ...Re8 and ...Be6 flexible; if White trades with 10.dxe5 dxe5 11.Qxd8 Rxd8 I'm completely fine, and 12.Nxe5 Nxe5 13.Rxe5 even loses to 13...Rd1+.

I checked 10.Nbd2 and saw it loses a pawn: 10...exd4 11.cxd4 Nxd4! 12.Nxd4 Bxd4 works because the knight on d2 blocks my queen's defence of d4 (my b6-bishop-facing pawn is then attacked twice, defended once). So I keep the d-file clear and play the useful prophylactic 10.h3, taking g4 away from both the bishop and the f6 knight while leaving d4 guarded by Nf3 and Qd1.

White's queenside pieces (Nb1, Bc1, Ra1) are still asleep, so I want to keep the central tension and add a defender/attacker on the e-file rather than release it with exd4. Re8 supports e5 and eyes e4; tactics like 11.Bxf7+ Kxf7 12.dxe5 dxe5 13.Nxe5+ Nxe5 14.Rxe5 Rxe5 just lose a piece for White.

The e5/d4 tension favours the space-gaining push 11.d5, which hits the c6 knight and is safely supported by the e4 pawn (Nxd5 just loses a piece to exd5). I checked dxe5 and Nxe5 lines: after dxe5 dxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 I have no recapture on e5 and drop a rook, so I avoid opening the e-file and close the centre instead, after which Na5 only drives my bishop to the safe c2 square.

White's d5 attacks my c6-knight, so I must move it; Nd4 loses a piece to Nxd4 exd4 cxd4 Bxd4 Qxd4, and Na5 leaves the knight offside after Bc2. Ne7 is the standard retreat in this closed Italian structure, keeping e5 solidly defended and rerouting the knight to g6 with ideas of Nh7/Nh5 and ...f5.

Bxh6 fails to gxh6 and Ng5 fails to hxg5 since the h6 pawn covers both squares, and Nxe5 just loses a piece to dxe5. Instead I play the thematic c4, cementing the d5 wedge, gaining space and preparing Nc3/Nbd2-f1-g3 while leaving no pawn tempo for Black.

The center is closed, so I want to redeploy my cramped e7-knight toward the kingside; Ng6 eyes f4/h4 and prepares Nh7 and ...f5 to fight for the initiative. I checked 12...Bxf2+ 13.Kxf2 Nxe4+ 14.Kg1, but the knight can't reach e1 from e4, so the sacrifice only nets two pawns for the bishop.

Bxh6 and Nxe5 both just lose a piece (g7 and d6 recapture), so I check quiet moves instead: Nbd2 develops my last piece, adds a second defender to e4 (currently attacked by Nf6 and held only by Re1), and prepares Nf1–e3/Nc4 plus the c5 or a4 expansion. I see no Black pawn push or capture that gains a tempo on it, and all my pieces stay defended (Bb3 by a2).

The knight jump 13...Nf4 is safe because White's Bc1 is blocked by the knight on d2, so the f4 outpost can't be challenged immediately; if White tries 14.g3 then 14...Nxh3+ 15.Kg2 Ng5 wins a pawn. It also eyes d3/e2 and supports a kingside build-up with ...Qf6 and ...g5 while the centre stays closed.

The natural 14.g3 fails because after g2 leaves, h3 is undefended and 14...Nxh3+ (or Bxh3) nets a clean pawn, so I reject it. Instead 14.Nf1 unblocks my c1-bishop with the concrete threat Bxf4 to eliminate Black's annoying knight, keeps h3 guarded by g2, and conveniently covers f2 so the ...Bxf2+ trick just loses a bishop to Nxf2.

White's Nf1 prepares g3 to kick my strong f4 knight, so instead of a knight sacrifice like Nxh3+ or Nxg2 (which only nets a pawn or two for a piece), I'll strike at the base of his pawn chain. After c6 dxc6 bxc6 I get a healthy central mass with d5 coming, my Bb6 stays active and his Bb3 goes passive.

My b3 bishop is entombed behind my own c4 pawn and is my worst piece, while Black's knight on f4 is his best, so trading them off is a clean positional gain; I checked that g3 immediately loses a pawn to Nxh3+ (g2 abandons h3) and that Nd4 drops a piece to exd4. After Bxf4 exf4, Black's only recapture, I have no loose pieces and can follow with Ne3/Nd4 to use the d5/f5 squares.

White's bishop just took my knight on f4, so the simplest and best reply is to recapture, restoring material balance. The pawn on f4 becomes an annoying wedge that restrains White's kingside and the e-file opens for my rook on e8 against White's Re1. Alternatives like Nxe4 fail to Bxe5 followed by Rxe4, leaving me a piece down.

Black's ...Nxe4 is a real threat since e4 is attacked twice (Nf6, Re8) but defended only by Re1, so I must add a defender. Checking enemy pawn captures first (rule 1) rules out Ng3 and Ne3, since the f4 pawn eats both squares; N1d2 develops my worst piece, gives e4 a second guard (Nxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 wins material for me), and keeps f2/b3 covered.

My f4 wedge is my main asset, so I want to make it permanent and keep the knight on f6 where it guards e4/d5 (killing the e5 push, since ...Nd7 would trade off any knight landing there). After 16...g5 the sac 17.Nxg5 hxg5 fails because my knight covers h5, and if 17.g3 fxg3 18.fxg3 I resolve my doubled pawn and get the e-file with ...Qe7/...Nh5 hitting g3.

Black's plan is ...g4 and a kingside pawn storm, so I want to challenge the cramping f4 pawn immediately: 17.g3 either wins it after fxg3 fxg3 (leaving Black's g5/h6 weak and opening the f-file for my rook) or meets ...g4 with hxg4, when I win a pawn and Black's structure collapses. I checked the tactics: ...Nxe4 fails to Nxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4, ...f3 is impossible because my knight sits there, and ...Bxf2+ Kxf2 fxg3+ Kxg3 just leaves me a piece up for two pawns; Nh4 would be a blunder since the g5 pawn takes it.

I noticed that 17...Bxh3 simply wins a pawn, since after 18.gxf4 gxf4 19.Kh2 my bishop retreats safely to g4 or d7 (no White piece controls g4 — the queen's path is blocked by Nf3), and 18.Qf1 would even lose the queen to Bxf1. I keep the strong f4 wedge and the open lines toward White's king while being a pawn up.

Black's real threat is ...fxg3, because with my king on g1 and his bishop on b6 raking the a7–g1 diagonal, the recapture fxg3 would be illegal (self-check), leaving a monster pawn on g3; likewise Kh2/Kh1 run into ...Ng4 with ...Nxf2 forking king and queen since Kxf2 is impossible. So I resolve the tension at once with gxf4, after which ...Qg5+ is blocked by his own knight on f6, ...g4 is met by Nh4 trapping the h3 bishop, and I can follow with Rf1 to shore up f2.

I checked 18...Nxe4, but after 19.Nxe4 Rxe4 20.Rxe4 I have no third attacker on e4 and simply lose a rook for a knight, so that's out. Recapturing with 18...gxf4 keeps material dead equal, opens the g-file toward White's king, and my h3 bishop has plenty of escape squares (g4, f5, e6) if White tries Kh2 to trap it.

Black's real threat is 19...Ng4, when ...Qg5+ and ...Bg2 crash through (e.g. Nd4? Ng4 Qg5+ Kh1 Bg2+! Kxg2 Qg4+ mating), so I must cover g4; Kh2 fails to 19...Ng4+ 20.Kxh3 Nxf2+ winning my queen. 19.Nh2 guards g4 and f1, keeps f2 defended, and unblocks f3 so that Qf3 next hits both f4 and the loose bishop on h3, whose only retreats g4 (knight) and f5 (e4-pawn) are covered.

My bishop on h3 is attacked by Nh2, and g4 is covered twice (Qd1 along d1–g4 plus the knight), so Bg4 and Ng4 both drop a piece; Be6 and Bf5 fall to dxe6/exf5, and Bxf2+ Kxf2 just loses the h3 bishop too. So I retreat it to the one fully safe square, keeping my extra pawn and the cramping f4 wedge.

I first checked the tempting checks: 20.Qg4+ and 20.Qh5 both lose the queen outright to ...Nxg4/...Nxh5 since the f6 knight covers both squares, and 20.Ng4 drops a piece because nothing recaptures on g4. Also, Black's f4 pawn captures on e3 and g3, so Re3/Qe3-type moves are out; Qf3 is attacked by nothing, guards g4 and f2's defender, and threatens Qxf4 to win my pawn back, which Black can't comfortably prevent.

White threatens Qxf4, and f4 can't be defended directly, so I want an active move: Bd4 is untouchable (Nd2 and Nh2 can't easily hit it) and threatens the undefended b2 pawn, while also preparing Be5 which would guard f4 (since Qxf4 would then run into Bxf4). After 21.Qxf4 Bxb2 22.Rab1 Be5 I hit the queen and stay a pawn up with the bishop pair; note Qg4+ never works for White because Nf6xg4 wins the queen.

f4 is undefended — no black pawn or piece covers it (Qd8's diagonal stops at h4, Nf6 and Bd4 don't reach), so Qxf4 wins the pawn and restores material equality while my queen also covers g4 and e4. If Black tries Bxf2+ Kxf2, I simply end up a bishop for a pawn ahead, and Bd4 remains loose for a future Ndf3 hit.

I noticed White's queen on f4 is eyeing the undefended h6 pawn (the g5 square is empty), so Qxh6 was a real threat; also my attractive-looking Bxf2+ tricks all fail because Qf4 guards f2 along the file. Kg7 defends h6 (and f6/f7), keeps my powerful bishop on d4, and White can't break with e4-e5 since Bd4 and Re8 overload the e5 square (e5 dxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 Qxe5 Bxe5 wins the queen).

I checked that d6 has no defender at all (Qd8 is blocked by its own bishop on d7, and no pawn or piece covers d6), so Qxd6 is a clean free pawn; I rejected 22.Ng4 because both Bd7 and Nf6 cover g4 (Bxg4 Qxg4 Nxg4 wins my queen) and rejected 22.e5 because ...Bxe5! hits my queen and the recapture costs rook for bishop. Black's only real counter is ...Bxb2, when Rab1 followed by Rxb7 or Nhf3 hitting the loose bishop keeps me on top.

White's queen on d6 is undefended, so 22...Qb8 attacks it (b8-c7-d6) while my queen is safely covered by Ra8, and it also guards b7 so that Bxb2 becomes a real threat with the rook joining on the b-file. Checks: 23.Qxb8 Rxb8 leaves b2 attacked twice and undefended, 23.Qf4 (hitting d4) is met by Be5 defended by my queen, and 23.Nf3 loses the queen to Qxd6 — unlike 22...Qe7, where 23.Qc7 hits b7 and a8.

My queen on d6 is attacked by Qb8 and most retreats lose it: Qxc6 falls to bxc6, Qe5/Qf4/Qg3+ all sit on the b8–h2 diagonal where g3/f4 are not really defended (f2 is pinned by Bd4 against my king, so Qg3+ Qxg3+! would just win my queen), Qc5 drops to Bxc5, Qe6 to fxe6, and Qc7/Qe7/Qf8/Qxd7/Qxf6 all hand over the queen. Since I am a clean pawn up with a strong d5/e4 wedge, the simplest consolidating move is to trade queens outright, killing Black's attacking ideas against my airy king; afterwards I will guard the loose b2 pawn with Rab1 and reactivate my knights via f3.

I'm forced to recapture the queen on b8, and taking with the a-rook keeps my e8 rook on the e-file pressuring e4 while the new b8 rook immediately threatens the undefended b2 pawn. With bishop pair plus active rooks against knights, this gives me the more comfortable game; Bxf2+ or Bxb2 first would just lose a bishop to Kxf2/Qxb2.

Black's Bd4 pins my f2 pawn (hence no f3/f4 available) and, more urgently, hits the completely undefended b2 pawn, so I fix my loosest point first; I checked that e4 is adequately held (Nf6+Re8 attack, Nd2+Re1 defend, so ...Nxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 wins a rook for a pawn) and that a2 is covered by Bb3. After Rab1 I stay a clean pawn up and can follow with Nhf3 to chase the d4 bishop and break the pin, which is simpler than 24.Ndf3 Bxb2 or 24.e5 Ne4 where Black grabs material or equalizes.

White's knight on d2 is loose and his king lacks pawn cover, so my strong bishop on d4 plus pressure down the e-file is my compensation for the pawn — note that f3 by White would run into ...Be3+ picking up the knight. Captures like Bxb2, Bxf2+, Nxd5 and Nxe4 all just lose material, so I improve with Re7, preparing to double rooks against e4 while keeping c6 guarding d5 and giving e5 extra support against Nf3.

Black's bishop on d4 is completely undefended, so Ndf3 develops with a direct attack on it while Nh2 guards f3/g4 (note Ng4 immediately would just drop a knight to Nxg4, and dxc6 would open the b-file making Bxb2 real). In every tactical try — 25...Nxe4, 25...Rxe4 or 25...Bxf2+ — I simply recapture and then take the loose bishop with Nxd4, staying a clean piece or pawn ahead.

My bishop on d4 is attacked by the knight that just arrived on f3 and is undefended, so captures like Rxe4 fail (26.Rxe4 Nxe4 27.Nxd4 wins a piece). Retreating to c5 keeps the bishop safe from pawn attacks for now, keeps the pressure on f2 along the a7–g1 diagonal, blocks c4-c5 and guards d6 against White's central pawn advance, and renews the real threat of ...Rxe4 since e4 is attacked twice and defended only by Re1.

I checked pawn captures first: Ng5 drops to hxg5 and Nd4 drops to Bxd4, while d6 just loses the pawn to Bxd6; e4 is currently held once by Re1, so I avoid loosening it with dxc6 Bxc6. Ne5 is attacked by nothing, centralizes, and hits both Bd7 (only defended by Re7) and f7, inviting the piece trade I want while a pawn up; if Black tries ...Bb4 hitting e1 I simply answer a3, and ...Nxe4 loses a piece to Rxe4.

Bd7 is attacked but defended by Re7, so there's no real threat; doubling with 26...Rbe8 adds a third attacker to the e-file and creates the genuine threat of ...Nxe4, since after Rxe4 Rxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 I win the pawn back and keep the bishop pair. White more or less has to concede ground with f3, and lines like 27.d6 Bxd6 or 27.Nxd7 Rxd7 only help me regain material.

I checked the tempting knight jumps and they all fail to captures — Ng6 drops to fxg6, Neg4/Nhg4 lose a piece because g4 is hit by both Nf6 and Bd7 while only defended once, Nxc6 falls to bxc6, and Re3 is simply met by Bxe3; also the e1 rook must stay to guard e4. So I play the simple consolidating developing move Nhf3, bringing my worst piece to the centre, defending Ne5 and covering d4/g5 while keeping my extra pawn and the strong d5/c4/e4 chain.

I checked the tempting 27...Bxf2+ 28.Kxf2 Ng4+, but 29.Nxg4! simply takes the checking knight and leaves me a piece down, so that's out; likewise Nxd5 and Nxe4 just drop material since both pawns are defended. Instead I'll resolve the central tension with cxd5, removing my weak c6 pawn (a target for dxc6 followed by Nd4/Ba4) and leaving White's bishop staring at its own light-squared pawns on d5 and e4, after which my bishop pair gets more play.

Black's new d5 pawn is attacked twice (c4 and e4) but defended only once (Nf6), so 28.cxd5 wins a clean pawn — if 28...Nxd5 then 29.exd5 (and 29.Bxd5 too) just takes the knight. I checked Black's counter-shots: Bxf2+ Kxf2 Nxe4+ loses to Rxe4, and Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 is a rook-for-knight loss, so capturing with the c-pawn also leaves me a protected passer on d5 supported by e4.

White's knight on e5 is attacked twice (Re7, Re8) but defended only once, since the e4 pawn blocks Re1 from the e5 square. So 28...Rxe5 29.Nxe5 Rxe5 wins two knights for a rook, and White's rook still can't take on e5; afterwards my two bishops plus knight dominate and the weak e4/d5 pawns fall (e4 is attacked twice, defended once).

Black's rook on e5 just took my knight there, and my Nf3 can recapture it — no black pawn covers e5, so the only recapture is ...Rxe8-rook from e8, giving me rook for knight and levelling the material count (two rooks plus bishop and five pawns against rook, two bishops, knight and four pawns). Alternatives like Nd4 just drop the knight to Bxd4, and leaving the rook alone lets Black grab e4 or d5, so the simple forcing recapture is clearly best.

I'm down material after Nxe5, so I need activity: Ng4 hits the e5 knight a second time (it's only defended by Re1, so Rxe5/Nxe5 would win a piece) while also adding a second attacker to f2 — with the knight guarding f2, Kxf2 is impossible, so Bxf2+ would win the rook on e1. If White grabs with Nxd7 I get Bxf2+ followed by Bxe1, recovering rook for bishop.

No black pawn or piece defends d7, so Nxd7 snaps off a bishop and simultaneously attacks the loose Bc5, meaning after any reply (…Re7, …Rd8, or the counter …Nxf2) I follow with Nxc5 and emerge two pieces up; …Rxd5 even loses the rook to Bxd5. This keeps things forcing rather than relying on a tactic, and the simple Nxg4 trade wins far less.

My bishop on c5 is hanging to the knight on d7, so moves like Rd8 or Nf6 just lose it to Nxc5; I need to save it actively. Bd4 is completely safe (nothing attacks d4), centralizes the bishop, and teams up with my knight on g4 to press f2 and b2, giving me some practical counterplay since I'm already down material.

My pieces on f2 and b2 are both attacked/loose (Bd4 and Ng4 hit f2, Bd4 eyes b2), so I play the simplest consolidating move: Re2 guards f2 and b2 along the second rank and is untouchable (Ne3 would just be met by fxe3). I rejected Nf6 (Kxf6), Nc5 and Ne5 (Bxc5/Bxe5) — all lose the knight to pieces guarding those squares — and Nb6 would needlessly concede f2.

I'm down a rook, so I need concrete counterplay: 31...f5 hits e4 twice (pawn and Re8) while the rook on e2 is actually undefended, so 32.exf5?? Rxe2 wins a rook back, and most other tries drop the e4 pawn. If White defends with 32.f3, my knight has good squares (Ne3 is poisoned since Rxe3 Bxe3+ regains the rook), so this is my best practical chance.

Black's real threat is ...fxe4, after which the e-file opens against my undefended rook on e2 (and exf5 immediately loses it to ...Rxe2), so I must shore up that file instead of grabbing material. Rbe1 doubles on e4/e2: now ...fxe4 runs into Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4, trading rooks while I stay a full rook up, and ...Bc3 is simply met by bxc3, while f2 has two attackers and two defenders so ...Nxf2 Rxf2 Bxf2+ Kxf2 only helps me.

I'm down a rook, so I need to generate activity and trades on the e-file rather than passively defend. Re7 hits the loose knight on d7 and sets a trap: if White tries Ne5, then Nxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 Rxe5 Bxe5 wins material back, and d6 fails to Rxd7.

Black's 32...Re7 attacks my undefended knight on d7, so I must save it — Ne5 and Nf6 lose to Rxe5/Kxf6, and ignoring it (exf5, d6) just drops a piece to Rxd7. Nc5 gets the knight to a safe square from pawns while hitting b7 and a6, and if Bxc5 I happily trade down while still a full rook and a pawn ahead (plus I retain the Ne6+ fork resource against Bd4 if Black kicks with b6).

I'm already a rook and pawn down, so simplifying won't save me — I need pawns and complications. Bxb2 grabs a free pawn (b2 isn't covered by the knight on c5, the bishop on b3 or the e-file rooks), and after tries like Nd3 or Rb1 I simply retreat with Bd4, keeping bishop and knight aimed at f2 while cutting White's material edge to just the rook.

Black's 33...Bxb2 grabbed a pawn but the bishop on b2 is completely undefended, and my rook on e2 reaches it along a clear second rank, so Rxb2 simply wins a piece by force and leaves me a full rook up. After Rxb2 the e4 pawn is still guarded by Re1 and f2 is covered by king and rook, so Nxf2 or Ne3 achieves nothing.

I'm down heavy material (rook for bishop), so I need to simplify and remove White's central pawn rather than grab at f2, since 34...Nxf2 35.Kxf2 just loses the knight for a pawn, and 34...Rc7 or Re6/Rd7 drop the rook to Ne6+/Nxd7/Nxe6. Taking on e4 eliminates a White pawn, keeps my rook active on the open e-file, and avoids immediate tactics.

I'm up a rook and bishop, so the simplest path is forced simplification: 35.Rxe4 is safe because e4 is covered twice (Re1 behind and Nc5), and no black pawn can touch it. After 35...Rxe4 36.Nxe4 all black counterplay disappears, and if instead 35...Nxf2 36.Rxe7+ then Kxf2 picks up the knight.

My rook on e7 is attacked by the rook on e4 and completely undefended, so I must deal with that first; Rxe4 just loses the rook to Nxe4 recapture and simplifies into a hopeless N-vs-much position. Since I'm already down material, I'll keep my rook safe and guarding the seventh rank with Rf7, where neither the bishop (blocked by d5) nor the knight can touch it.

The black knight on g4 is completely undefended (no pawn on h5, rook on f7 doesn't cover it), and Rxg4+ comes with check along the g-file so Black has no time for counterplay. That wins a clean piece by force, leaving two rooks, bishop and knight against a lone rook — the simplest consolidation.

I must move out of the rook check, and since I'm already down material I want my king active rather than passive on the h-file. Kf6 keeps the f7 rook protected, blockades the f-file, and lets my king head for e5 to pressure the d5 pawn; White's checks (Ne4+, Rf4+) don't win anything.

I'm up two rooks, a bishop and a knight, so I want the simplest safe consolidating move rather than a flashy fork — Nd7+ drops the knight to Rxd7, Rf4+/Rg6+ give the rook away to the king, and Ne4+ lets ...Kf5 hit both knight and the undefended rook. Instead d6 advances my passer with knight support, leaves nothing loose, and Black has no checks or captures at all (the f7 rook is blocked by its own king, so Rxf2 is impossible).

The d-pawn is the main danger, and 37...Rd7 loses to Nxd7+ while 37...Rc7 doesn't stop d7 since the knight guards it. Putting the rook on f8 keeps it behind the pawn so that after d7 I can meet it with Rd8 and blockade the promotion square.

Nd7+ is check from the knight while simultaneously attacking the rook on f8, and d7 is attacked by nothing black has. The king's only legal square is f5 (e6/f7 are covered by Bb3, e7 by the d6 pawn, g-squares by Rg4), so I simply win the rook with Nxf8 next.
I'm in check from the knight on d7 and Kf5 is the only legal move, so there's nothing to calculate beyond playing it.

Black's rook on f8 is already attacked by my knight on d7, but immediate Nxf8 allows Kxg4 since my rook on g4 is undefended; Be6+ both guards g4 along the diagonal (so Kxg4 is impossible) and forces the king to move, after which Nxf8 wins the rook outright. Every legal king reply (Kf6, Ke5, Kxe6) leaves the f8 rook lost, so I win material by force rather than by a loose fork.
Only one legal move is available — the bishop check on e6 must be answered, and capturing with the king is forced.

Nd7 forks nothing complicated — Nxf8+ is check and simply captures Black's only piece, with no pawn or piece able to recapture on f8. That leaves me two rooks and a knight against three bare pawns, the simplest forced win rather than any clever maneuver.

I'm down a lot of material, so I should grab what I can and keep my king active — d6 is undefended (the knight on f8 doesn't cover it, nor do the rooks), so Kxd6 wins the dangerous passed pawn. Kf7 attacking the knight just lets it escape (Nd7) while the d-pawn keeps running, so taking the pawn is clearly better.

I'm up two rooks and a knight against bare pawns, so I just need a forced ladder mate rather than anything clever. Rg6+ drives the king off the 6th rank (the h6 pawn captures on g5, not g6, so the rook is untouchable), and after e.g. Kd7 Rxb7+ Kd8 Rg8# the mate comes quickly, while Rb6+ would let Kc7 attack my undefended rook.

I'm hopelessly behind in material, so I want to grab anything I can: Ke7 steps out of check while attacking the undefended knight on f8, since Rg6 doesn't cover that square. White will likely save the knight with Nh7 or Nd7, but Ke7 is the only move that poses any threat and keeps my king active and centralized.

Black's last move Ke7 attacks my undefended knight on f8, and tricks like Re6+ or Rg7+ fail because Kxe6 wins the rook and Kxf8 is still available after Rg7+. Nh7 is the only square where the knight is both safe (no black piece or pawn covers h7, and Kg7 is impossible due to my rook on g6) and keeps my full extra material of two rooks plus knight for a trivial win.

new_lessons: [middlegame] Count the full capture sequence on a square, not just defender numbers: if two enemy rooks hit a knight defended by a knight, you lose two pieces for one rook Example: 26.Ne5 with black rooks on e7/e8: Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 won two knights for a rook

[middlegame] If your piece is already hit by stacked heavy pieces, trade it off or retreat it at once; adding a cheap defender only feeds the exchange sequence Example: 27.Nhf3 "defended" Ne5; 27.Nxd7 was needed, instead Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 collected both knights

[middlegame] Do not push g3/h3 or move pawns in front of your king while an enemy bishop eyes h3/g2; keep the shield and break in the centre instead Example: 17.g3 invited fxg3 and Bxh3, shredding my king; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[middlegame] Answer a wing pawn storm with the central pawn break or file-opening capture, not with a defensive pawn move on the attacked wing Example: Facing ...g5-g4, 17.g3 lost; dxc6 or e5 opened lines toward Black's king first

[middlegame] Before any piece move, list every enemy pawn that can capture the destination square; a pawn defender or capturer refutes forks and centralisations Example: ...Qc3 forked rooks but bxc3 took the queen; Ng5 and Nd4 ideas died to hxg5, Bxd4

[middlegame] For each candidate, name the opponent's best capture or pawn push reply before choosing; if any wins material or tempo, pick another move Example: ...d5 and ...f5 chased my bishop with no retreat; bxc3 refuted Qc3

[middlegame] Each move, list your undefended pieces and squares where one enemy move hits two of them; fix the loosest before starting anything active Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn handed Black free tempo moves ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5

[middlegame] With a material edge, play the simplest consolidating move and trade pieces (not pawns); refuse clever knight tours that leave pieces loose Example: A piece up, Be4 instead of Nc3 threw away most of the advantage in two moves

[middlegame] Keep a knight or bishop on an advanced central square only when a pawn can support it; otherwise it is a target chased by pawns or rooks Example: Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns because c4/d3 support never arrived

[opening] Before an exchange sequence on an open file, recount the defenders of your central pawn after every trade has been made Example: 8.a4 axb5 axb5 Rxa8 removed e4's guard and lost the pawn to ...Nxe4

[middlegame] Cover enemy entry squares (c2, d3, g4, your sixth rank) with a pawn or piece before invaders arrive; never trade queen for rook voluntarily Example: Opponent's rook reached d6/c6 freely; ...Qc3 bxc3 turned a crushing attack into a lost grind

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected and mutually defended, and choose the recapture that keeps the chain linked even if it doubles a pawn Example: 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6 and Rd6-b6-a6 ate them; bxc4 held everything together

[endgame] Never let a lone bishop be the sole defender of your pawns: a rook attacking it forces a losing trade and the whole queenside falls Example: 33.Rd6/34.Rc6 hit the b6 bishop until Bd6 Rxd6 won bishop and every pawn

[endgame] Before your king grabs material on the edge, count the pawn race and confirm your king stays inside the square of every enemy passer Example: 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f4-f5-f6 and h-pawn promoted two unstoppable queens

[endgame] Before simplifying, name the exact ending you enter and confirm it is a known win; bishop plus two pawns versus rook is usually only a draw Example: Trading into rook-versus-bishop after Qc3 was objectively lost despite "extra pawns"
